Clearly, what's there now isn't good, but we will need to decide what the fix is, i.e. should the software using the client be able to directly control the HTTP config (and wire or pass it in) or should the client handle it internally?
is this something that can be fixed by configuration?  I'm not familiar with all of the bells-and-whistles that are in HttpClient 4.x.

, sorry, no, what I meant was "Does the client take responsibility for this or does it demand that the user of the client provide it with some ready-assembled HTTP apparatus to use?" Neither alternative fixes your problem, but the fix for your problem should be written differently depending on which choice we make.
I don't know if there is config in HttpClient for this kind of thing. Maybe some kind of timeout system?

I don't know for sure either.  IIRC, there is a mechanism for evicting connections, but an aggressive eviction policy is probably not the optimal solution.
As you say, agreeing on whom is responsible for connection management would be the appropriate first step.  If the FcrepoClient is responsible, it may be reasonable to:
1. Upon FcrepoClient receiving an HttpResponse from Fedora, read the response body from HttpResponse, and keep it in memory.  This frees the connection to Fedora.
2. Provide the copy of the response body on the FcrepoResponse.

Updating FcrepoOperationFailedException to include the entire FcrepoResponse may not be a bad idea (so the user of FcrepoClient has full access to anything in the response that may clue you into the cause), but not necessary if the FcrepoClient is freeing connections by reading the HttpResponse body.
It could be dangerous to cache the response body in the case of large bitstreams.
I agree that including a reference to the response object in any exceptions is just good practice no matter what.

I agree that caching could be dangerous, but that's exactly what is happening now, right?  I mean, right now, the large bitstream is attached to the HttpResponse, and I'm proposing that the large bitstream be attached to the FcrepoResponse.  Obviously, there's the impact copying bytes around.

What about something akin to allowing the user of FcrepoClient to provide a function to read the response body off of the HttpResponse directly?  Maybe there are overloaded methods for each of get(...) post(...) etc.  If the user of FcrepoClient is concerned about the overhead of copying bytes, they can use the overloaded method to handle the HttpResponse body directly (and are responsible for closing connections by reading it)?  Otherwise FcrepoClient copies the response body (using the existing/non-overloaed get(...), post(...) etc methods).

InputStream

FcrepoResponse
implement
AutoCloseable

try-with-resource
idiom. Most IDEs will then offer advice or a warning if the client-using code fails to manage the response correctly.

It is unclear whom is responsible for managing HTTP connections that are created by the FcrepoClient on behalf of the user.  Presumably the FcrepoClient is, but in my environment I'm running across the following issues:

1. Connections are only released if the user of FcrepoClient reads the response body.  If the user of the FcRepo client does not read the response body, the FcrepoClient eventually blocks waiting for a free connection.

2. If an FcrepoOperationFailedException is thrown, the user of FcrepoClient has no access to the response body, and cannot free the connection.  If enough exceptions are thrown, the FcrepoClient will eventually block waiting for free connections
A PR demonstrating the issue follows.
See:
https://github.com/fcrepo4-exts/fcrepo-java-client/issues/5
